newsitem.title: FRANCE: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER WINS AS FERRARI TAKE CONTROL.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER WINS AS FERRARI TAKE CONTROL.

text.p: Michael Schumacher opened up a clear 14-point lead in the battle for the world drivers' championship on Sunday with a convincing and comfortable victory for Ferrari in the French Grand Prix.

Schumacher, winner of the title in 1994 and 1995 for Benetton, outclassed all his rivals and contradicted his own predictions by finishing 23 seconds clear of fellow-German Heinz-Harald Frentzen in a Williams.

It was the Schumacher's second successive victory, his third in four races and the 25th of his career -- a total which lifts him level with Briton Jim Clark and Austrian Niki Lauda in the record books.
Only Alain Prost (51), Ayrton Senna (41), Nigel Mansell (30) and Jackie Stewart (27), have won more Grands Prix.

Schumacher now has 47 points in the drivers' championship, ahead of Canadian Jacques Villeneuve of Williams on 33 and Frentzen on 19 and has an excellent chance of claiming his third title despite all his protestations to the contrary.

"Obviously I was wrong in what I said before this race," he admitted afterwards. "I just hope I am wrong again about the British Grand Prix at Silverstone. We were terrible there in the test, so I just hope we can improve as much as we did from the test here before this race."

In a generally predictable race enlivened by changing weather conditions which resulted in two accidents on the final lap, Schumacher's Ferrari team mate Briton Eddie Irvine finished third to consolidate the Italian team's grip on the constructors' series.
They now have 65 points to Williams' 52.
Villeneuve, who spun off and recovered after attempting to lunge past Irvine on the last lap, finished fourth, ahead of Frenchman Jean Alesi in a Benetton and 21-year-old Ralf Schumacher in a Jordan.

The younger Schumacher owed his single point to the thoughtfulness of his brother, who slowed down to allow him to unlap himself by passing him at the final corner of his penultimate lap, and also some luck.
This came in the form of Alesi trying to dive past Briton David Coulthard into fifth place on the final lap, a move which succeeded but sent Coulthard and his McLaren spinning out of the race.
"What happened?" said Coulthard afterwards. "Alesi happened....But he has apologised now, so I suppose that has to be okay doesn't it."

The drama of the closing moments and also the finishing order was at odds with the previous 70 laps of entirely predictable racing in which the cars drove around in a neat procession interrupted only by the pit-stops.
The first lap saw world champion Damon Hill of Britain lose all hope of a reasonable finish by being pushed out at the first corner into the gravel.
This meant forced him to limp back to the pits for a new nose and front wing section and he finished the race 12th and last of the cars that were still running.
"It was spitting with rain all the time," he said. "So it was always very marginal."

The conditions made it difficult, but not impossible and resulted in some of the leading drivers pitting for intermediate tyres which became problematic for them at the end of the race as the circuit dried out. This was why there were crashes on the final lap.

"I am satsified as I needed a finish and second is okay," said Frentzen. "But I know it is not what everyone expected. It is difficult and Ferrari are very strong, despite everything Michael keeps saying about them struggling."
Irvine confirmed that despite the fact his contract is due for renewal at the end of July -- when Ferrari's options on him expire -- he still wants to stay with the team.
"I am not looking around for anything else," he said. "We are on top of both championships and that's pretty good."
